newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels stand firm as world pressure grows.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels stand firm as world pressure grows.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 103 VIP hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima stood firm on Friday in defiance of growing international pressure for a solution to the 10-day-old crisis.

A stream of pleas from around the world were ignored as the heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels showed no sign of softening their conditions for releasing hostages from the booby-trapped residence.

In Japan, whose nationals account for the largest number of hostages after Peru, the government urged the world's strongest nations to join forces to end the hostage crisis. Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference Japan had started talks with Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations to draft a common strategy to end the standoff at the residence in Lima.

"It is clear that the international community should not condone terrorism. It is also necessary ... to act as one to help resolve this crisis by setting free all the hostages peacefully, and at an early date," Ikeda said without giving more details.

German Foreign Ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann told Reuters G7 ambassadors had already met in Lima to discuss their next step. He said Russia was also taking part in the talks. "The main objective is to prevent violence," Erdmann said.

The G7 moves followed Christmas pleas from around the world, including Pope John Paul II and U.S. President Bill Clinton, for the rebels to soften their hearts. The guerrillas have freed three hostages since a mass release of 225 on Sunday, keeping those they consider most useful as bargaining chips including two Peruvian ministers, Japanese businessmen, a handful of foreign diplomats and the brother of President Alberto Fujimori.
They are demanding the release of around 400 jailed comrades in Peru, followed by safe passage -- with some hostages as guarantors -- to an Amazon jungle stronghold.

Fujimori, who has spoken in public just once since the rebels stormed a party at the ambassador's residence on Dec. 17, refused to negotiate with them directly and has flatly rejected their demand for prisoner releases. He also ignored pleas by hostages to reconnect electric and water services to the building.
He has also rebuffed foreign offers of help, and Russian leader Boris Yeltsin's suggestion to send a special G7 task force to free the hostages brought no official response from Lima.
Crack Peruvian troops have drawn up a plan to storm the residence as a last resort, but police sources warn another MRTA unit in Lima is ready to strike other targets if this happens.

Former hostages have warned against trying to overpower the guerrillas, who are armed with grenades, other explosives and ample ammunition. Defiant rebels appeared at windows several times on Thursday holding up automatic rifles and flashing victory signs to camera lenses trained on the residence.
On Friday morning, witnesses said they could see a man cleaning the interior of the building with a broom but reported no other movement at the site.

A former hostage, medical doctor Victor Lucero Rondon, said in a newspaper interview on Friday three of the captives were running serious health risks. Dominican Republic Ambassador Victor Lucero Rondon suffered from diabetes, Peruvian Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja had a high-risk heart condition, and Energy and Mines Vice Minister Juan Mendoza had a hernia.
